## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/02.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Conceptualizing Academic Impact
• The pandemic and all the ensuing disruptions functioned/
functions as an “academic headwind”, impeding (in general) the
academic progress of students.
• Headwinds impede progress in two ways:
• They slow one’s rate of progress
• And by slowing one’s rate of progress they lead to less distance being
travelled.
• In education these two impediments manifest as:
• Decrease in student growth.
• Decrease in student attainment.
RI Academic Impact Discussion 2021</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/03.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">RICAS SGP Operational Considerations in 2021
• Due to no RICAS testing in Spring 2020, RICAS growth analyses will be
skip-year/gap year growth from 2019 to 2021.
• Two types of SGP analyses were conducted for RICAS data:
• Cohort referenced analyses: These analyses create growth norms from the
2019 to 2021 students. These growth norms yield cohort means/median
SGPs of 50 and obscure COVID-19 academic impact.
• Baseline referenced analyses: Historical growth norms were created using
2019 and prior data. These growth growth analyses don’t have mean/median
SGPs of 50 and can be used to investigate overall COVID-19 academic impact
• Projections (lagged and straight) were calculated for 2021 data using
baseline growth norms in case they were needed.
RI Academic Impact Discussion 2021</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/04.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">WIDA-ACCESS SGP Operational Considerations in 2021
• Two types of SGP analyses were conducted for WIDA-ACCESS data:
• Cohort referenced analyses: These analyses create growth norms from the
2020 to 2021 students. These growth norms yield cohort mean/median SGPs
of 50 and obscure COVID-19 academic impact.
• Baseline referenced analyses: Historical growth norms were created using
2020 and prior data. These growth growth analyses don’t have mean/median
SGPs of 50 and can be used to investigate overall COVID-19 academic impact.
• Use composite score from WIDA-ACCESS data. No analyses performed
using sub-scores.
• Projections (lagged and straight) were calculated for 2021 data using
both cohort and baseline growth norms in case they were needed.
RI Academic Impact Discussion 2021</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/05.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">SGP Summary of Cohort versus Baseline Referenced
• Cohort referenced SGPs
• Growth norms created from the current cohort of students.
• Mean/median will by 50 for all grade x content area analyses
• Cannot investigate overall impact of the pandemic on students.
• Can investigate differential impact of the pandemic on students.
• Does not require scale stability across years.
• Baseline referenced SGPs.
• Growth norms created from historical (i.e., pre-COVID) cohorts of students.
• Mean/median 50 for historical cohort, not necessarily 50 for current cohort.
• Extent of deviation from (i.e. below) 50 is indicative of less learning/pandemic related
academic impact.
• Mean SGP deviation of 5 corresponds to an effect size of 0.18.
• Can investigate BOTH overall impact and differential impact
• Requires scale stability across years.
RI Academic Impact Discussion 2021</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/06.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">SGP Assumptions
• SGP analyses presume valid scale scores
• Students forming the growth norm group are presumed to have taken the same (or
equivalent) test at the same time. Scores have to mean the same thing.
• SGPs, however, are often used as a post-hoc check of scale score validity/
comparability via Reductio ad absurdum
• In 2021, check form comparability and mode-of-administration comparability.
• RIDE has extensive experience (e.g., PARCC paper/pencil versus online) investigating
and accommodating mode-effects.
• If scores are not comparable then we either attempt to make them comparable or
run separate analyses.
• We assume something close to population invariance with respect to IRT
scaling.
• The population of students tested in 2021 and differences to 2019 is a concern
so we begin with data on the population of students tested.
RI Academic Impact Discussion 2021</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/09.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">SGP Analyses for 2021
• With comparable results we can quantify pandemic related
academic impact:
• At the state level
• Demographic subgroups including ethnicity, poverty
• Academic subgroups (special education, low/high achievers)
• By region/district/school
• By mode of education (remote/hybrid/in-person).
• Attendance
• English Language Learner impact can be evaluated using WIDA-ACCESS
results.
RI Academic Impact Discussion 2021</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/14.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Discussion
• Median baseline SGPs in ELA were in the mid 30s and median baseline SGPs in
mathematics were lower (upper teens to lower 30s).
• Deviation from normal growth (i.e., 50) represents the extent to which
academic growth slowed down from 2019 to 2021, that is, academic impact.
• Larger academic impact in ELA than mathematics.
• Academic impact is fairly uniform across grades.
• Academic impact is very large likely requiring multiple years and additional
educational supports/interventions to recover.
• Recovery implies getting back (at a minimum) to where 50th percentile growth would
have led to.
• Median/mean growth below 50 must be averaged out with median/mean growth
above 50 going forward. E.g. A mean two-year SGP of 35 would need to be followed
by mean two-year SGP of 65 in order to get an average of 50.
RI Academic Impact Discussion 2021</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/16.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Discussion of Grade Level Results
• Median baseline SGPs are low in elementary school grades and
are close to 50 in the high school grades.
• Deviation from normal growth (i.e., 50) represents the extent to
which academic growth slowed down from 2020 to 2021, that is,
academic impact.
• Academic impact is very large in elementary and middle school
and close to non-existent in high school.
• Lack of impact is consistent with:
• Great academic support for the group during the pandemic.
• Impoverished learning conditions prior to the pandemic such that the pandemic
didn’t alter the status quo.
RI Academic Impact Discussion 2021</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/18.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Discussion of Ethnicity Results
• Broken out by ethnicity, 2021 baseline SGP results show similar
rank ordering (i.e., growth gaps) as seen in normal years.
• Student academic growth is lower in mathematics than in ELA
for all ethnic subgroups.
• Even though growth is lower for ethnic minorities, academic
impacts (growth difference with 2019) are uniform across
ethnicity subgroups.

RI Academic Impact Discussion 2021</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/35.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Discussion of Growth by Prior Achievement Results
• In some grades and content areas median SGP baselines vary by the
prior achievement level of students, sometimes substantially.
• For example, in Grade 6 ELA lower achieving students had much lower
baseline SGPs than higher achieving students. This implies that those
students had much greater academic impact.
• In Grade 7 mathematics higher achieving students had lower baseline
SGPs than lower achieving students implying that higher achieving
students were more impacted.
• In general, there is a fairly uniform impact by prior achievement level.

RI Academic Impact Discussion 2021</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/36.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Participation Rates and Interpretation
• An issue impacting the interpretation of growth (and status) results in
2021 is participation in the state assessment.
• Low participation doesn’t impact calculation of cohort referenced
growth norms nor use of baseline referenced growth norms.
• Low participation does impact comparisons of group level results with
historical (e.g., 2019) results based upon higher participation rates.
• For example, how should one compare growth and status results for
school in 2019 and 2021 with very different rates of participation.

RI Academic Impact Discussion 2021</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/37.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">School Level Results
• Due to larger fluctuations in participation rates a the school level, growth
comparisons between 2019 and 2021 must be approached more cautiously.
• In general we have found via multiple imputation that comparisons of status
and growth results from 2019 to 2021 are defensible.
• Whether a school’s results support cross-year comparison depends more on
the size of the school than on the participation rate/enrollment change.
• The following are academic impact results at the school level:
• For grades 3 and 4, academic impact was determined via status change analyses.
• For grades 5, 6, 7, and 8 academic impact was determined via growth change.
• Summarization across grades within a school was done by averaging ordinal levels of
impact (Severe 5, Large 4, Moderate 3, Modest to None 2, and Improvement 1)

RI Academic Impact Discussion 2021</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/42.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">SGP Analysis Plans post 2021 (2022 and beyond)
• Spring 2021 represents an ideal time to get a snapshot of student
attainment as we are hopefully/presumably at or near the point
of maximal impact on student attainment.
• That is, recovery has not really begun for most students in
earnest.
• It’s impossible to talk about recovery sensibly without
understanding how big the impact is.
• Monitoring recovery will be at least as critical as monitoring the impact of
the pandemic on student achievement.
• Beware the K-shaped recovery!
RI Academic Impact Discussion 2021</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/43.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Summary of Findings
• Academic impact analyses were successfully conducted for both RICAS and
WIDA-ACCESS.
• Results of the analyses suggest large academic impacts on students due to
the pandemic.
• Results are larger in math and in ELA
• Results are uniformly large across most demographic subgroups.
• Results show variation across academic subgroups (e.g., high versus low
achievers in some content areas).
• Academic impact varied greatly by schools and also varied by 2018-2019 STAR
Rating.
• Recovery from impacts this large will likely take multiple years and require
additional supports beyond that provided by normal schooling.
RI Academic Impact Discussion 2021</div>
```
